Emphysema subtypes & grading — quick reference

Centrilobular — small, ill-defined lucencies clustered around the centrilobular core structures, upper-lobe predominant, no visible wall. The smoking-related pattern. Visual grading here runs Trace → Mild → Moderate → Confluent → Advanced destructive as the lucencies enlarge, coalesce, and progressively destroy the lobular architecture.

Panlobular — uniform, diffuse destruction of the whole secondary pulmonary lobule with simplification of the vasculature, classically lower-lobe predominant. Look for this in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Paraseptal — subpleural lucencies abutting the pleura or fissures, a single layer thick, sparing the lobular core. Graded here as Mild vs. Substantial by extent. Important because confluent paraseptal disease is the substrate for spontaneous pneumothorax, and it can mimic a thin-walled cystic lesion (TWCL) or the subpleural cysts of UIP/honeycombing — the key discriminator is wall thickness and lack of a fibrotic reticular background in paraseptal emphysema.

Bulla — an emphysematous airspace >1 cm with a wall <1 mm. A giant bulla can compress adjacent lung (compressive atelectasis) and must be distinguished from a pneumothorax, since management differs — look for visible, often curvilinear bulla wall and preserved (if crowded) vessels within the compressed lung, versus a sharp visceral pleural line with no lung markings peripheral to it in a pneumothorax.

General teaching framework — provided as a reference for interpreting the categories tested here, not a case-specific diagnosis.
